summary: This article, an author-manuscript version of a J Breath Res paper by Pleil, Geer Wallace, Davis and Matty, explains the physics and physiology of human breathing across normal, on-demand, and ventilator conditions. It covers tidal volume, minute ventilation, oxygen saturation, altitude effects on partial pressure of oxygen, CO2 tolerance in artificial atmospheres such as spacecraft and submarines, respirators and masks, high-flow oxygen therapy, and extreme breath-holding. The note is truncated before its on-demand and SCUBA sections are complete.
one_line: A physics-focused overview of human breathing parameters, oxygen and CO2 levels, altitude, protective masks and medical oxygen support across different environments.
key_facts: At complete rest, the typical adult male exchanges approximately 0.5 L of air per breath at 12 breaths per minute, a minute ventilation of about 6 L per minute.
The first 0.15 L of each breath, referred to as the tracheal dead volume, does not participate in O2/CO2 exchange.
Pulse oximetry readings of SpO2 between 95 and 100% are considered normal; 90% or below indicates hypoxemia.
At sea level, the partial pressure of oxygen (ppO2) is 0.21 atmospheres; Mexico City at 7,350 feet has ppO2 of 0.16 atm, about 60% of sea-level O2 density.
Commercial airliner cabins are pressurized to an equivalent altitude of about 8,000 feet (0.16 ppO2 atm) as mandated by Federal Regulation 14 CFR 25.831.

FAA general aviation guidelines require supplemental O2 if cabin pressure drops to 12,500 feet equivalent (0.13 ppO2 atm) for more than 30 minutes and always above 14,000 feet cabin altitude (0.12 ppO2 atm).
The article states that the altitude tipping point for unassisted breathing in very fit individuals is around 26,000 feet.
ASHRAE standard for CO2 in offices is 800 ppm (0.08%), though levels of 4,000 to 5,000 ppm have been measured.
CO2 concentrations of 100,000 ppm and above can cause loss of consciousness and asphyxiation.
NASA's spacecraft maximum allowable concentrations (SMACs) for CO2 for 1-h and 24-h exposure were set at 13,000 ppm; the CO2 SMAC was later removed.
The highest recorded spacecraft CO2 level was 14.9 mmHg on Apollo 13.
Low-flow oxygen therapy delivers up to 15 liters per minute and can deliver up to about 80% fraction of inspired oxygen.
High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) can deliver up to 60 LPM and range up to 100% O2.
Free divers without prior oxygen loading can routinely hold their breath for 10 minutes or more and dive unassisted to 300 feet.
The human record for breath holding with O2 loading is 24 minutes 37 seconds, achieved by Budimir Šobat in Sisak, Croatia in March 2021.
